title: Review: Tide Tables, Poems That Know Exactly How Clever They Are
paragraphs: Chidinma Eze's first collection of poems, Tide Tables, arrives with the kind of reviews that publishers frame and poets avoid reading. 'Dazzling', says one newspaper. 'Fearless', says another. I admit that I picked up the book with a faint hostility, as one approaches a dinner guest whose entrance has been announced too loudly. It is to the collection's credit that the hostility lasted only about forty pages, and to its discredit that it returned for the last sixty.

The premise is elegant. Each of the forty poems is named after a date in a fictional harbour town's almanac, and each pairs a tide with a memory: a drowned bicycle, an aunt's unpaid debts, a conversation in a language the speaker no longer speaks. The sea, in these poems, is less a setting than a method. It returns what we give it, a little altered, and never at the hour we expected. At its best, this produces lines of startling economy, such as 'the water keeps the receipt'.

Eze is also genuinely funny, which is rarer in poetry than critics admit. A poem about a failed driving test turns, in its final three lines, into an argument about forgiveness, and does so without any visible effort. Another, addressed to a neighbour's loud parrot, manages to be both an elegy and a complaint. These are the moments when the poet forgets to be admired and simply pays attention, and the results are the strongest in the book.

Unfortunately, forgetting is not Eze's habit. Too many poems pause, mid-line, to remind us how well they are doing. A metaphor is introduced, explored and then politely explained, as though the poet feared that a reader might miss it. There is a recurring gesture, a final line that turns the whole poem on its heel, which is thrilling the first four times and conspicuously mechanical by the twelfth. One begins to see the machinery, and machinery, however well oiled, is not what we come to poetry for.

Defenders will argue that self-awareness is the hallmark of the age, and that a poet who can see her own tricks is more honest than one who cannot. The point is fair. Yet honesty and display are not the same thing, and the best self-conscious poets, one thinks of writers who laugh at their own devices, make the laughter part of the poem. Eze, by contrast, seems to expect applause for noticing, which turns a sophisticated insight into a rather expensive form of vanity.

None of this should discourage a reader from buying the book, which at the equivalent of twelve pounds is considerably cheaper than a decent lunch and far more durable. The best dozen poems will repay many rereadings, and the sequence about the aunt's debts, which I will not spoil, is quietly devastating. It is simply that one wishes the poet would trust her material as much as her gift. A talent this large does not need to keep announcing itself at the door.

I suspect that Eze will write a better book than this one, and that she will know, when she does, which sentences to leave alone. Meanwhile, Tide Tables remains a remarkable debut with the remarkable flaw of being aware of it. It is rare to criticise a poet for being too talented, but then Eze has been generous enough to provide the occasion. The sea, after all, returns what we give it, and she has given it everything, including its own commentary.

questions.explain_es: Dice que 'Eze is also genuinely funny' y que los momentos de atención sencilla son 'the strongest in the book'.

options: He thinks it is too long for a short collection

questions.explain_es: Inferencia: la llama 'quietly devastating' y la incluye en 'the best dozen poems'.

options: Playfully critical, with a touch of admiration

questions.explain_es: Tono: retoma la imagen del mar para decir con humor que Eze se entregó por completo, incluso con comentario propio, lo que es su defecto.

options: figuratively, to suggest a high cost to the poems
literally, to refer to the book's price

title: The City Should Not Sleep Without Its Cleaners
focus: Modal verbs of obligation and persuasive structure
paragraphs: At half past two in the morning, a woman named Rosario Huamán waits at a bus stop in the south of Lima. She has just finished cleaning an office tower in Miraflores, where, for a few hours, she tidied the desks of people who are asleep in other districts. The next bus on her route will not arrive until five. She will spend the intervening time standing on a pavement, clutching her bag and avoiding the eyes of strangers. This is not an unusual night. It is, for thousands of Limeños, the night.

The city's transport system, like most in the region, was designed for those who work between nine and six. It runs best when it is least needed, in the daylight and in the centre, and thins out as the hours become dangerous or inconvenient. The people who rely on it at night are not a marginal minority. They are nurses, bakers, security guards, cleaners and delivery drivers, the very people whose work makes the daytime city possible, and who are punished for it with the longest and riskiest journeys.

Some will say that a night service cannot pay for itself. They are right, and it should not be expected to. Public transport is not a business; it is an infrastructure, in the same sense that streetlights and drains are infrastructure. Nobody demands that a pavement turns a profit. What we should ask is whether the service reaches the people who need it and whether the cost, shared among all taxpayers, is a fair price for a city that functions for everyone, including those who work while the rest of us sleep.

The practical objections are weaker than they sound. A modest night network, limited to six or seven main routes and running once an hour, would cost a fraction of what the city has spent on a single flyover. It could be funded in part by a small supplement on fares during the day, which most passengers would barely notice. Several cities in Latin America and elsewhere have introduced similar services and found that demand, once reliable, grows faster than expected.

There is also a question of safety, which cannot be solved by a timetable alone. A bus that arrives every hour is better than none, but a stop with no lighting and no other people is still a dangerous place. Stops on the night routes should be well lit, shelters should be built where people are most likely to wait, and drivers should be trained and supported in dealing with harassment. None of this is extravagant. It is simply what a serious service looks like.

Critics may respond that the money should go to taxis or to cheap loans for motorbikes. But this only repeats the logic that has failed so far: leave each worker to solve, privately and at her own expense, a problem that the city has created. A woman who earns a few hundred soles a week should not have to spend a tenth of it on a taxi simply to reach her bed. That is not a free market. It is a tax on exhaustion.

The municipal council meets next month to approve the transport budget. We urge its members to include a pilot night network, and to judge it after a year by one simple measure: how long people like Rosario spend waiting in the dark. If the answer is less than before, the experiment will have justified itself. If not, the council will at least have discovered, honestly, what the city is prepared to ask of those who clean up after everyone else.

questions.explain_es: Sostiene que 'it should not be expected to': el transporte público es infraestructura, como las aceras.

questions.explain_es: Inferencia: son 'the very people whose work makes the daytime city possible' y reciben 'the longest and riskiest journeys'.

options: Sharp and indignant
Hesitant and uncertain
Humorous and light
questions.explain_es: Tono: es una frase breve y contundente que expresa indignación ante la injusticia de que el trabajador pague privadamente.

options: To explain the history of the bus network
To criticise one particular employer
To make a general problem human and concrete

options: Ignores them completely
Anticipates them and answers each in turn
Accepts all of them as conclusive
questions.explain_es: Estructura: aborda el coste, la seguridad y las alternativas (taxis, motos) y responde a cada objeción.

options: a small trial version
a luxury service

title: The House in Montevideo
focus: Narrative tenses, reported speech and subtext
paragraphs: The agent arrived at eleven, which gave Lucía and her brother an hour to disagree about the kitchen. Their father had died in March, and the house in Pocitos, with its sea-green shutters and its stubborn lemon tree, now belonged to both of them in equal parts. The estate agent had suggested a price in the region of eight million Uruguayan pesos. Joaquín had already spent it, in conversation, on a flat in Madrid and a second-hand car.

'We cannot keep it,' Joaquín said, running a finger along the dusty counter. 'Neither of us lives here. It costs money every month. Be realistic.' Lucía, who lived forty minutes away and had visited every Sunday for six years, said nothing. She was not being realistic. She was looking at a small pencil mark on the door frame, beside which her father had written, in capitals, JOAQUÍN, 1998.

The agent, a brisk man named Facundo, walked through the rooms with a tablet and an expression of professional neutrality. He praised the light, noted the damp in the corridor and observed, as though announcing a diagnosis, that houses like this one 'sell themselves'. Lucía wondered whether a house can sell itself against its own wishes. She followed him upstairs, opened the window of her old bedroom and discovered, taped to the glass, a note she did not remember writing.

It said, in a child's handwriting: DO NOT SELL. THIS IS ALSO MY HOUSE. She laughed, aloud and unexpectedly, and had to sit on the bed. At the age of nine she had been furious about something, probably a lost game, and had made the decree on the spot. Her father, who never threw anything away, had evidently decided to honour it for twenty-five years, leaving the note exactly where she had put it.

'What's funny?' Joaquín called from the corridor. She did not answer. Instead she peeled the note from the glass, folded it twice and put it in her pocket, a gesture that struck her as ridiculous and absolutely necessary. When he came in, he looked at her face and then, a little unwillingly, at the window. For a moment, neither of them spoke, and it occurred to her that this was the first silence they had shared since the funeral.

They sold the house in the end. It would be sentimental, and false, to pretend otherwise. Joaquín was right about the costs, and Lucía, to her own surprise, was relieved when the final signature was done. But on the afternoon before the keys changed hands, she took the lemons from the tree, filled two bags and drove her brother to a small café where, to his bewilderment, she asked the owner to make lemonade from them.

'It's Papá's recipe,' she told him, when it arrived. 'He used to add salt.' Joaquín tasted it, grimaced and then, slowly, smiled. 'It's terrible,' he said. 'It's exactly right.' They drank it in the sun, side by side, saying very little. In her pocket, the child's note had grown soft at the folds. She had no intention of ever showing it to anyone, and she suspected that her father, wherever he was, had counted on exactly that.

questions.explain_es: El texto dice que vivía a cuarenta minutos 'and had visited every Sunday for six years'.

title: The Last Edition
paragraphs: Colleagues, friends, and the few readers who, I am told, have come to check that we are really closing: good evening. For thirty-one years I have worked in this building, and for the last eleven I have been its editor. In all that time I have never been asked to give a speech, which suggests either that I am not eloquent or that my colleagues were wise. Tonight, since the building has been sold and the printing presses are to become a car park, I find that I am free to be both.

Let me say first what we were not. We were not the richest newspaper in Buenos Aires, and we were not the most famous. We never had a correspondent in every capital, and our offices were cold in winter and hotter than the sun in summer. In the best years we paid our reporters badly, and in the worst, I am ashamed to say, we paid them late. If you are looking for a business model, I would advise you to look elsewhere.

Let me say next what we were. We were the paper that sent a young reporter, Camila Ferreyra, to a flooded neighbourhood in the south of the city and printed what she found, even when it embarrassed a minister. We were the paper that corrected its mistakes on the second page, in the same size of type as the mistake, because a correction that is hidden is only a second lie. We were, for three decades, a small and stubborn promise: that somebody was checking.

I want to thank the people who kept that promise. I thank the sub-editors who read every comma twice, usually at two in the morning and usually without thanks. I thank the photographers who ran towards the things that others ran away from. I thank the people in the print room, whose hands smelled of ink and who taught me that a newspaper is, before anything else, a physical object that someone must carry and someone must pay for.

I am not going to pretend that the closing of a newspaper is a tragedy for everyone. Some will say, and they will not be entirely wrong, that the news now arrives faster and cheaper from a thousand sources, and that nostalgia is an expensive habit. But I would ask them to consider what is lost when a city has a thousand voices and no one whose job it is to check which of them is true. Speed is not the same as knowledge, and volume is not the same as truth.

To the young journalists in this room, some of whom are not yet thirty, I owe an apology and a hope. The apology is that we leave you a profession in poor repair, with fewer salaries, fewer desks and a public that has been taught to distrust the very people who warn it. The hope is that you will build something better, and that you will not wait for permission. The tools are now yours. The standards, I trust, are ones you already understand.

In a few minutes, I shall go to the press room and watch the final copies come off the machine. I have promised myself that I will not cry, a promise I expect to break, probably by the second page. Thank you for the years, for the arguments, for the coffee that no one ever described as drinkable. And if, tomorrow, you find a mistake in anything that I have said tonight, you know exactly where to look: on the second page, in the same size of type.
glossary: editor de redacción, corrector de estilo

questions.explain_es: Lo dice: 'corrected its mistakes on the second page, in the same size of type as the mistake'.

Bitter and accusing

options: To blame the owners for selling the building
To announce a merger with a larger newspaper

options: condition
price

title: A Beginner's Guide to Sounding Clever in Meetings
paragraphs: Many young professionals assume that intelligence is the most valuable quality in a meeting. This is a charming error, and one that may take years to unlearn. In truth, what is valued is the appearance of intelligence, which is cheaper, quicker and, with practice, indistinguishable from the real thing. The following guide, based on the author's long and unrewarded experience in Toronto offices, will help you achieve this without having to read any of the documents.

Rule one: speak last, but not too last. The person who speaks first risks being wrong; the person who speaks after everyone else risks being unnecessary. The ideal moment arrives when the discussion has begun to circle, when three colleagues have said the same thing in different words and everybody is quietly checking the time. At that moment, lean forward, pause and say, 'I wonder whether we are solving the right problem.' It has never failed, since nobody knows what the right problem is.

Rule two: master the vocabulary of motion. Nothing in a modern company is ever done; it is moved forward, taken offline, circled back to or unpacked. A project is never late, only 'on a longer runway'. A failure is 'a learning'. A disagreement is 'a healthy tension'. When confronted with a question you cannot answer, say that it is 'a great question' and that you would like to 'take it away', after which you may safely forget it, as everybody else will.

Rule three: use numbers sparingly, but with confidence. A figure delivered quietly, without a source, is far more persuasive than a chart. Try, 'The data suggests about thirty per cent.' If challenged, add that the figure is 'directional'. This word has the remarkable property of meaning nothing at all, and has therefore never been proved wrong. Should you be asked to share the data, say that you will 'circle back', and refer to rule two.

Rule four: employ the strategic nod. A slow nod, accompanied by a thoughtful look at the ceiling, can be held for up to eight seconds and is understood by most listeners as agreement, wisdom or both. Advanced practitioners add a small frown, which conveys that they have found a subtle problem and are generously choosing not to mention it. At no point should you reveal whether you have understood. Mystery, as every manager knows, is a form of authority.

Rule five: whenever possible, bring a notebook and write nothing in it. A closed notebook signals preparation; an open one with nothing written signals attention; one with a few words, ideally underlined, signals insight. Do not, under any circumstances, write down the word 'lunch'. Colleagues who observe such an entry may suspect that your thoughts have wandered, which, naturally, they have, but they must never be given evidence.

In conclusion, the aspiring professional should remember that none of these techniques requires talent, effort or knowledge. That is their enormous advantage. Within a year you may expect to be invited to more meetings, to a more senior role and, eventually, to chair meetings of your own, where you will hear the same sentences from the young and, to your quiet astonishment, find yourself nodding. Good luck, and please, take this away and circle back to me.
glossary: dar vueltas; volver una y otra vez
pista; margen de tiempo o recursos

questions.q: The guide recommends that a speaker should always talk first in a meeting.
questions.explain_es: La regla uno dice lo contrario: 'speak last, but not too last'.

They often reward the appearance of insight over real work

options: Deadpan and mock-serious
Sentimental and nostalgic
Angry and confrontational
questions.explain_es: Tono: finge dar consejos serios para ridiculizar una cultura laboral de apariencias.

options: To give a real deadline for a project
To use the jargon it has just mocked, as a final joke
To criticise the reader's lack of attention
questions.explain_es: Propósito: el final reproduce la jerga ('take it away', 'circle back') y cierra con ironía circular.

questions.q: How is the text organised?
options: As a numbered series of rules ending in a conclusion
As a chronological account of one meeting
As a dialogue between two managers
questions.explain_es: Estructura: parodia el formato de una guía práctica con reglas numeradas y conclusión.

questions.q: In 'Mystery, as every manager knows, is a form of authority', 'mystery' refers to…
options: telling long stories at work
solving a hidden crime
not revealing what one thinks or knows
questions.explain_es: Aquí 'mystery' es ambigüedad deliberada: no revelar si se ha entendido.

title: In Defence of the Mediocre Hobby
topic: Amateur pursuits and the pressure to excel
paragraphs: Last spring, a friend of mine in Medellín confessed that she had taken up watercolour. She said it with the sheepish tone of someone admitting to a crime, and she followed it at once with a disclaimer: she was terrible at it, she would never show anyone the results and she was only doing it for herself. I found this sequence of statements more interesting than the paintings, which, when I finally saw them, were mediocre in exactly the way she had promised.

Her apology, I realised, is the habit of our age. We have been taught that every activity must be justified by an outcome. A hobby must become a side income, a run must become a marathon, a blog must become an audience. The idea that one might do something simply because it is pleasant, and do it badly for years, has begun to seem faintly suspect, as if time could only be spent respectably when it had been invested.

The internet has not helped. It displays the best work of millions of people, instantly and without context, so that the beginner no longer compares herself to her neighbour but to the finest practitioner on the planet. Against such a standard, any amateur effort looks like failure. Yet the comparison is absurd: nobody who enjoys cooking expects to be judged against a restaurant with three stars. We have simply forgotten that the audience for most human activity is, or ought to be, the person doing it.

The benefits of mediocre pursuits are, I think, underrated. To do something badly and carry on is a rare and useful form of courage. It trains us to tolerate being a beginner, a condition many adults avoid completely, preferring to remain good at things they already know. It also keeps us humble. The person who has spent a year failing to draw a hand will never again regard a drawn hand, in any gallery, as a trivial achievement.

There is a social dimension as well. Amateurs, unlike professionals, have no competitive reason to protect their methods, and so they talk. The amateur choir, the village football team, the evening class in pottery: these are among the few places where people of different ages and incomes still meet on equal terms, joined only by a shared incompetence. It is hard to be pompous when you have just dropped a vase. A society with fewer such places is, I suspect, a more anxious one.

I should not be misunderstood. I do not claim that excellence is overrated, and I would not want my surgeon to regard her profession as a pleasant way of passing the afternoon. There is nothing wrong with ambition, and many hobbies do grow into something larger. My point is only that the reverse is also legitimate: that some things are better for being left small, and that a pastime does not have to graduate into a career to be worth the paint.

My friend still paints on Thursday evenings. She has not improved much, and she has stopped apologising, which is the real progress. Last month she gave me a small picture of a cup on a windowsill, in which the cup is lopsided and the window slightly sad. It hangs above my desk. Whenever I fail at something of my own, I look at it, and I find, to my surprise, that I want to try again.

questions.q: The author's friend showed her paintings to many people with pride.
questions.explain_es: Ella dijo que 'she would never show anyone the results'; el texto la describe con tono avergonzado.

questions.q: The author claims that doing something badly can build courage.
questions.explain_es: Dice que 'To do something badly and carry on is a rare and useful form of courage'.

questions.q: What can be inferred about the picture of the cup?
options: It was bought at a gallery in Medellín
It was painted by a professional artist
It matters to the author because of what it stands for
questions.explain_es: Inferencia: cuelga sobre su escritorio y le da ganas de intentarlo de nuevo; simboliza la libertad de hacer algo imperfecto.

questions.q: What is the author's attitude towards the pressure to turn hobbies into careers?
options: Gently critical
Neutral and detached
Fully approving
questions.explain_es: Actitud: la ve como un hábito de la época que vuelve 'faintly suspect' el placer, y lo critica con suavidad.

questions.q: Why does the author mention surgeons in the sixth paragraph?
options: To prevent a misreading of her argument
To argue that doctors should paint
To explain how surgeons choose hobbies
questions.explain_es: Propósito: aclara que no desprecia la excelencia ('I should not be misunderstood').

questions.q: How does the essay open and close?
options: With a statistic and a prediction
With two different anecdotes of no relation
With the same friend, first apologising and later no longer doing so
questions.explain_es: Estructura circular: comienza con la disculpa de la amiga y termina con que 'she has stopped apologising'.

questions.q: In 'the internet has not helped', the word 'helped' is used…
options: to mean that it paid for the hobby
with enthusiasm for new technology
with understatement, since the internet made things worse
questions.explain_es: Eufemismo: dice que 'no ha ayudado' para indicar que ha empeorado la autocomparación.

title: How Zero Travelled
topic: History of mathematics and the number zero
paragraphs: It is difficult to imagine mathematics without zero, and yet for much of human history it did not exist as a number. People counted objects, and nobody counts nothing. Ancient civilisations did sometimes need a mark to show an empty place, as in the difference between 'fifty-three' and 'five hundred and three', but a placeholder is not yet a number. The real invention, which was to treat nothing as something that can be added, subtracted and multiplied, took centuries to arrive.

Historians generally agree that a decisive step was taken in India. In the seventh century, the mathematician Brahmagupta set out in writing rules for arithmetic with zero, stating, for example, that a number added to zero remains unchanged. His treatment of division by zero was less successful, and mathematicians would argue about it for a very long time. Still, the principle was in place: zero was no longer merely an absence but a quantity with properties of its own.

The Maya, meanwhile, had independently developed a positional counting system that included a symbol for zero, often drawn in the shape of a shell, which they used in their calendars. Whether it functioned as a full number in the modern sense is debated, but the achievement is not in doubt. It is a useful reminder that great ideas are not always passed along a single road, and that humans in distant places can arrive at similar solutions to similar problems.

From India, the concept travelled westward through scholars writing in Arabic. The mathematician al-Khwarizmi, working in Baghdad in the ninth century, described the Indian system of numerals and its use of a place-value notation. His name, in Latinised form, eventually gave us the word 'algorithm'. The word 'zero' itself is believed to descend, through Italian, from the Arabic term sifr, which also gave English the word 'cipher'. Language, like arithmetic, bears the marks of the journey.

Europe, to be candid, was slow to be convinced. The Italian mathematician Fibonacci introduced the Hindu-Arabic numerals in his book Liber Abaci, published in 1202, and merchants gradually recognised their advantages. Yet authorities in several cities were suspicious. Some forbade the new numerals in official accounts, partly because a zero could easily be altered into a nine, and partly, one suspects, because the Roman system was familiar and the new one seemed alarmingly foreign.

The suspicion proved short-lived, because the practical benefits were overwhelming. Multiplying large numbers in Roman numerals is an ordeal; in the place-value system, it is a routine exercise. Without it, there would be no efficient bookkeeping, no decimal fractions and, many centuries later, no binary code, in which everything on a computer is built from zeros and ones. The tiny circle that once alarmed medieval officials now sits at the heart of every device we use.

Perhaps the most interesting aspect of the story is not who invented zero but why it was so hard to accept. A number that stands for nothing seems almost philosophically scandalous, and many thinkers resisted it for that reason. What the history suggests is that the most powerful ideas are often those that require us to think differently about the obvious. Nothing, it turns out, was waiting to be noticed all along, and noticing it changed absolutely everything.

title: Review: The Quiet Embassy, a Film of Beautiful Evasions
topic: Film as literary adaptation and political allegory
paragraphs: The Quiet Embassy, adapted by the Chilean director Valentina Rojas from a novel of the same name, is a film about a country that is never named and a crisis that is never explained. A young diplomat, Mateo, arrives to take up a post at a small embassy, where nobody will tell him what he is supposed to do. Corridors are long, telephones ring in distant rooms and the ambassador, a gracious woman who seems to age with each scene, speaks exclusively in proverbs. It is an unusual, patient and frequently beautiful piece of work.

I should say at the outset that the adaptation is intelligent. The novel, which is narrated from the diplomat's point of view, depends on the reader's slow suspicion that he is not telling the whole truth. Rojas solves the problem by keeping the camera slightly behind his shoulder, so that we see what he sees but never his face at the key moments. It is a cinematic equivalent of an unreliable narrator, and one of the best I have seen.

The visual design deserves the praise it has received. Cinematographer Inés Carvajal, working largely in the greys and pale greens of old government buildings, makes the embassy seem less a place than a mood. Every frame is composed with a care that approaches fastidiousness. A scene in which Mateo eats lunch alone, watched by a portrait of a president whose name is never mentioned, is a small masterpiece of unspoken menace, and it contains not a single line of dialogue.

Unfortunately, the film is not content to leave its allegory implicit. In the last half hour, a minor character delivers a monologue explaining, in meticulous detail, what the embassy 'really' represents: a state whose institutions have continued to function after losing their purpose. This is a reasonable reading, and the audience has been moving towards it for ninety minutes. To have it announced, however, is rather like having a joke explained by the person who told it.

Performances are uniformly strong. As Mateo, Daniel Ibarra gives a study in controlled bewilderment, his eyebrows doing more work than most actors' entire bodies. The ambassador, played by veteran Marta Echeverría, is the film's great success, in part because she is allowed to be ambiguous: it is never clear whether her proverbs conceal wisdom or merely cowardice. The tension between those two possibilities carries much of the film, and I suspect it will outlive the monologue.

Some viewers have complained that nothing happens, and it would be dishonest to pretend that this is entirely untrue. Yet I think the complaint misses the point. The film's subject is not an event but a condition: the experience of belonging to a structure that no longer knows what it is for. A conventional plot would have betrayed that subject. What is more debatable is whether the film needed to be quite so long, and a trim of twenty minutes would have done it no harm.

I recommend The Quiet Embassy, with reservations that I hope are clear. It is a film for patient audiences and those who enjoy being unsettled rather than reassured. It will not change the world, nor does it seem to want to, which is perhaps the most diplomatic thing about it. But it will remain with you in the way that a half-heard conversation remains: incomplete, a little disturbing, and strangely hard to forget.

title: The Wrong Wedding
topic: Mistaken identity, hospitality and unexpected belonging
focus: Narrative tenses, comic understatement and dialogue
paragraphs: It was entirely the fault of the invitation, Andrés would later insist, which had been printed in a script so ornate that the street number looked like a sneeze. He had been asked to a wedding in Quito by a former classmate, Julián, and he had arrived at the church at four exactly, in a borrowed jacket, carrying a gift worth thirty dollars and a slightly nervous smile. Only after he had sat down did he realise that he did not recognise a single person, including the bride.

He decided to wait. A man who has arrived at the wrong wedding, he reasoned, has two options: to leave, which is conspicuous, or to stay, which is merely strange. The woman beside him, a large and cheerful person in a lilac hat, leaned over to whisper that the groom's family always took a long time. 'You are on the bride's side, aren't you?' she asked. Andrés, who had never said no to anyone in a hat, said that he was.

The ceremony was beautiful. He felt it would be impolite not to say so, and so, as people filed out into the sun, he told the woman in the lilac hat that he had been deeply moved. She was delighted. She told him that he must come to the reception, and she told it to him the way people in Ecuador tell a guest he must eat, as a matter beyond discussion. Fifteen minutes later he found himself at a table of strangers, being served a plate of fritada with such force that he did not dare refuse.

The difficulty was that everyone assumed he was somebody's cousin. Andrés tried several times to explain, but each attempt was interrupted by an aunt, a toast or a plate. By the third course, he had been introduced as a doctor, an engineer and, briefly, a relative of the bride's godfather. He learned that the bride, Paola, was a veterinarian, that the groom was frightened of horses and that the family was extremely proud of its cheese. He found, with some alarm, that he was enjoying himself.

At half past nine, a boy of about ten sat down beside him and said, with the clarity of a customs officer, 'You are not from our family.' Andrés, who had been waiting for this, confessed everything in a whisper. The boy considered the matter, ate a piece of cake and said, 'My uncle also came to the wrong wedding once. He stayed twenty years.' He pointed across the room to a very happy man with a very large moustache, who waved.

It was then that Andrés's phone buzzed. It was Julián, writing from another church on the other side of the city, where, it appeared, a wedding had been waiting for its missing guest for five hours. 'Where ARE you?' the message said. He typed an answer, deleted it and typed another, and found that every version sounded like a lie, which was unfortunate, since for once it was the truth.

In the end, he went to both receptions, arriving at the second after midnight with a cheese in a plastic bag, a present from the first. Julián forgave him within a minute, partly because he was tired and partly because nobody can be angry with a man carrying cheese. Years later, Andrés still receives a Christmas card from Paola's family, addressed to 'our cousin'. He has never corrected them, and he has never once forgotten to reply.
